categories.category: Plan, Implement, and Manage a Lakehouse

question.title: OneLake Architecture
question.scenario: A retail company is migrating their data platform to Microsoft Fabric. They have data from 15 different source systems including SAP, Salesforce, and on-premises SQL Server databases. The data engineering team wants to establish a single storage layer that all Fabric workloads can access without data duplication. They need to organize data by business domain (sales, inventory, finance) with different access controls per domain.
question.question-text: Which OneLake architecture best organizes multi-domain data with proper isolation?

choices.choice: A single lakehouse with folders per domain and row-level security on all tables
Separate workspaces per domain, each with their own lakehouse, using OneLake shortcuts for cross-domain access where authorized
A single workspace with separate SQL endpoints per domain for access control
Multiple Fabric capacities — one per domain — with no cross-access capability

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about how Fabric workspaces provide security boundaries and how shortcuts enable controlled cross-domain access.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Separate workspaces per domain provide workspace-level security boundaries with distinct role assignments (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer). Each workspace has its own lakehouse with domain-specific Delta tables. OneLake shortcuts create virtual references to data in other workspaces without copying — access is governed by the source workspace permissions. This provides domain isolation with controlled cross-domain analytics when authorized.

ul.li: OneLake is a single logical data lake for the entire organization — all Fabric items store data in OneLake automatically.
Shortcuts support references to: other lakehouses, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, AWS S3, and Google Cloud Storage.
Workspace roles cascade to all items within — separating domains into workspaces provides clean RBAC boundaries.
OneLake data access roles (preview) provide object-level security within a lakehouse for finer-grained control.

question.title: Dataflow Gen2 vs Pipeline
question.scenario: A data engineering team needs to ingest data from a REST API that returns paginated JSON responses, transform the nested JSON into flattened tabular format, apply business logic (currency conversion, date normalization), and load the results into a lakehouse Delta table. The process runs every 4 hours and typically processes 500,000 records per batch.
question.question-text: Which Fabric data movement approach is most appropriate for this scenario?

choices.choice: Data Pipeline with Copy Activity and mapping data flows for transformation
Dataflow Gen2 with Power Query for extraction, transformation, and direct lakehouse destination
Spark notebook triggered by a pipeline schedule for all steps
Eventstream for real-time ingestion from the REST API

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Consider which tool handles paginated REST API extraction with complex transformation at the 500K record scale efficiently.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Data Pipeline with Copy Activity natively handles REST API pagination (supports both offset and cursor-based patterns) and can extract JSON at scale. Mapping data flows provide a visual transformation layer for flattening nested JSON, applying business logic, and writing to Delta tables — optimized for batch processing at scale. Dataflow Gen2 uses Power Query which is excellent for smaller datasets but less performant for 500K records with complex transformations. Pipelines also provide better orchestration, retry logic, and monitoring.

ul.li: Copy Activity REST connector supports: pagination rules, request headers, OAuth2 authentication, and response flattening.
Mapping data flows run on Spark clusters under the hood — handling millions of records efficiently.
Dataflow Gen2 Power Query mashup engine is memory-bound — 500K records with complex transforms may hit limits.
Data Pipelines support parameterization, dynamic content expressions, and error handling patterns (retry, timeout, conditional paths).

question.title: Semantic Model Relationships
question.scenario: A financial analyst is building a semantic model for sales analysis. The model has a fact table (Sales) with 100 million rows connected to dimensions: Date, Product, Store, and Customer. Some reports need to show sales by product category AND by customer segment simultaneously. The analyst notices that filtering by customer segment does not filter the product category totals correctly in a matrix visual.
question.question-text: What is the most likely cause of the incorrect filtering behavior?

choices.choice: The model uses Import mode instead of DirectQuery for the fact table
The cross-filter direction on the Sales-to-Customer relationship is set to "Single" instead of "Both"
The fact table is missing a relationship to one of the dimension tables
The relationships between dimensions are bidirectional, causing ambiguous filter paths

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When multiple dimensions are filtered simultaneously through a fact table, consider how filter direction ambiguity can cause unexpected results.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Bidirectional relationships between dimensions create ambiguous filter propagation paths — a filter on Customer Segment can reach Product Category through multiple paths (Customer > Sales > Product vs. a potential direct dimension-to-dimension relationship). DAX evaluates ambiguous paths unpredictably. The correct pattern is single-direction relationships from dimensions to facts (many-to-one, single direction) which ensures filters flow cleanly through the star schema without ambiguity.

ul.li: Star schema best practice: all relationships one-to-many from dimension to fact, single cross-filter direction.
Bidirectional relationships should be used sparingly — only when required for specific DAX patterns (e.g., many-to-many bridging).
Use CROSSFILTER() DAX function to temporarily modify filter direction in specific measures rather than setting bidirectional globally.
Performance impact: bidirectional relationships increase model complexity and can degrade query performance on large tables.

question.title: SQL Analytics Endpoint
question.scenario: A business analyst team needs to run ad-hoc SQL queries against lakehouse Delta tables without affecting data engineering workloads. They use tools like Azure Data Studio and SSMS. They need read-only access with T-SQL syntax support, including views for commonly used queries. The data engineering team does not want analysts to consume Spark compute capacity.
question.question-text: Which Fabric feature provides SQL-based read access to lakehouse data without consuming Spark resources?

choices.choice: Creating a warehouse and importing data from the lakehouse
The lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint with T-SQL views and warehouse-style compute
A Spark notebook with spark.sql() queries shared with analysts
A KQL queryset connected to the lakehouse via shortcuts

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Every Fabric lakehouse automatically has a companion endpoint that provides SQL-based access — what is it called?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The SQL analytics endpoint is automatically created for every lakehouse in Fabric. It provides a read-only T-SQL interface over Delta tables using a SQL engine (not Spark) — consuming SQL compute capacity separately from Spark jobs. Analysts can connect via SSMS, Azure Data Studio, or any ODBC/JDBC tool. It supports creating views, stored procedures (read-only), and granting object-level permissions — perfect for analyst self-service without impacting engineering workloads.

ul.li: SQL analytics endpoint auto-syncs metadata from Delta tables — no manual schema refresh needed.
It supports T-SQL syntax including CTEs, window functions, and cross-database queries within the same workspace.
Compute is separate from Spark pools — SQL queries use the Fabric SQL engine with its own capacity allocation.
Object-level security (table/view permissions) and column-level security can be configured on the SQL endpoint independently.

question.title: Capacity Management
question.scenario: A company purchased an F64 Fabric capacity shared across 5 workspaces. During month-end processing, the finance workspace consumes so much compute that other workspaces experience throttling and job failures. The platform team needs to prevent any single workspace from starving others while still allowing burst capacity when available.
question.question-text: Which Fabric capacity management approach prevents workspace resource starvation?

choices.choice: Upgrade to F128 capacity to provide headroom for all workspaces
Implement smoothing and throttling rules with capacity metrics monitoring and workspace-level compute caps
Reduce the number of concurrent jobs in the finance workspace manually
Move the finance workspace to a separate Fabric capacity with dedicated F32

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: When one workspace consistently needs guaranteed capacity that impacts others, the cleanest isolation is physical separation.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Assigning the finance workspace to its own dedicated F32 capacity provides guaranteed compute isolation — finance month-end processing cannot impact other workspaces regardless of load. The remaining workspaces share the original capacity without contention from finance jobs. Fabric capacities are the unit of compute isolation; within a single capacity, all workspaces compete for the same CU pool. This approach provides predictable performance for both finance and other teams.

ul.li: Fabric capacities use CU (Capacity Units) — all workload types (Spark, SQL, Dataflow, Power BI) share the same CU pool.
Throttling occurs when background CU consumption exceeds the capacity limit — jobs are delayed or rejected.
Fabric capacity metrics app shows CU utilization, throttling events, and per-workspace consumption breakdowns.
Capacity smoothing spreads burst consumption over time (24-hour window) but cannot prevent sustained over-consumption.

question.title: Delta Table Optimization
question.scenario: A lakehouse Delta table stores 2 billion rows of IoT sensor data partitioned by date. Queries that filter by sensor_id (which is not the partition column) perform full partition scans taking 45 minutes. The table receives 10 million new rows daily via append operations. File sizes vary from 1MB to 500MB due to small batch appends throughout the day.
question.question-text: Which combination of Delta optimizations will most improve query performance for sensor_id filters?

choices.choice: Repartition the table by sensor_id instead of date
Increase the Spark executor memory to cache the full table in memory
Create a materialized view filtered by sensor_id and schedule hourly refresh
Apply OPTIMIZE with ZORDER on sensor_id, and enable V-Order for the table to improve read performance

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Z-ordering co-locates data by a column within files, enabling file skipping — and V-Order optimizes file layout for read performance.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: OPTIMIZE compacts small files (solving the 1MB-500MB variance from small batch appends) into optimal-sized files. ZORDER BY sensor_id co-locates rows with the same sensor_id within files, enabling data skipping — queries filtering by sensor_id only read files containing that sensor's data rather than scanning all files in a partition. V-Order is a Fabric-specific write optimization that sorts data within Parquet row groups for faster reads across all Fabric engines (SQL, Spark, Power BI).

ul.li: OPTIMIZE compacts files to target size (~1GB in Fabric) — reducing the number of files scanned and metadata overhead.
Z-ordering creates min/max statistics per file for the z-ordered column — enabling file-level predicate pushdown (data skipping).
V-Order applies special sorting within Parquet row groups optimized for the Fabric Verti-Scan engine — 10-50% faster reads.
Best practice: OPTIMIZE with ZORDER as a scheduled maintenance job (nightly) after daily appends complete.

question.title: Medallion Architecture
question.scenario: A healthcare organization is implementing a medallion (bronze/silver/gold) architecture in their Fabric lakehouse. Raw data arrives from 20 source systems in varied formats (CSV, JSON, Parquet, HL7 FHIR). They need to track data lineage, handle late-arriving data, apply data quality rules, and produce curated datasets for reporting. Schema changes in source systems should not break the pipeline.
question.question-text: Which implementation of the medallion architecture best handles schema evolution and data quality?

choices.choice: Bronze: raw files in Files section as-is; Silver: schema-enforced Delta tables with merge schema enabled; Gold: aggregated views with data quality checks via notebooks
Single lakehouse with all three layers in the same set of tables using column prefixes (bronze_*, silver_*, gold_*)
Three separate Fabric capacities — one per medallion layer — with cross-capacity queries
Skip bronze entirely and load directly to silver with strict schema validation that rejects non-conforming records

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Bronze preserves raw data as-is (schema-agnostic), silver applies structure with schema evolution support, gold curates for consumption.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Bronze layer stores raw files in the lakehouse Files section without schema enforcement — preserving the original data regardless of format changes. Silver layer uses Delta tables with mergeSchema option enabled, which automatically adds new columns when sources evolve without breaking existing pipelines. Gold layer applies data quality rules (completeness, accuracy, consistency checks) and creates curated, business-ready aggregations. This three-layer approach provides full lineage (raw to curated) and resilience to schema drift.

ul.li: Delta Lake mergeSchema: set spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true or use .option("mergeSchema", "true") on writes.
Bronze Files section supports any format — landing zone for ELT pattern where transformation happens downstream.
Data quality rules in gold can use Great Expectations, custom Spark assertions, or Fabric Data Quality Rules (preview).
Late-arriving data: use Delta MERGE (upsert) at silver layer with watermark columns to handle out-of-order arrivals.

question.title: DAX Calculation Groups
question.scenario: A financial reporting semantic model has 50 measures (Revenue, COGS, Gross Margin, Net Income, etc.) that each need time intelligence variants: Year-to-Date, Prior Year, Year-over-Year %, and Moving Average. Creating individual measures for each combination would result in 200+ measures, making the model difficult to maintain and confusing for report authors.
question.question-text: Which DAX modeling technique reduces measure proliferation while providing all time intelligence variants?

choices.choice: Calculation groups with calculation items for YTD, PY, YoY%, and Moving Average that apply to any base measure dynamically
Create all 200+ measures with consistent naming conventions and organize in display folders
Create a single SWITCH measure that accepts a parameter to select the time intelligence type
Use report-level measures in Power BI instead of model measures

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Calculation groups apply time intelligence patterns to ANY measure dynamically — creating the variants without duplicating measure logic.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Calculation groups create a virtual dimension with calculation items (YTD, PY, YoY%, Moving Average). When applied to any measure, the calculation item modifies the evaluation context — TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, etc. are applied dynamically. You maintain only the 50 base measures plus 4 calculation items (54 total instead of 200+). Report authors drag the calculation group column into visuals to select which time intelligence variant to display. Maintenance is centralized — updating the YTD logic updates all 50 measures simultaneously.

ul.li: Calculation groups use SELECTEDMEASURE() to reference whatever measure is in context — making them generic.
Precedence: when multiple calculation groups exist, the ordinal property determines application order.
Calculation items can use ISSELECTEDMEASURE() to apply different logic for specific measures (e.g., skip YoY% for ratio measures).
Available in Tabular Editor, ALM Toolkit, and natively in Power BI Desktop (Model view) for Fabric semantic models.

question.title: KQL Database for Real-Time Analytics
question.scenario: A logistics company needs to analyze real-time GPS telemetry from 50,000 delivery vehicles. They need sub-second query response for: current vehicle positions (last known location), route deviation alerts (comparing actual vs planned route), and historical trip analysis over the past 7 days. Data arrives at 100,000 events per second during peak hours. Older data should be archived to the lakehouse for long-term analytics.
question.question-text: Which Fabric real-time analytics architecture handles this ingestion rate with the required query latency?

choices.choice: Stream data directly to lakehouse Delta tables and query with Spark SQL
Direct ingestion to a Power BI streaming dataset with real-time dashboard
Dataflow Gen2 running every minute to append data to a warehouse table
Eventstream ingesting to a KQL database with hot cache for 7 days, OneLake availability enabled for automatic archival to lakehouse

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: KQL databases are optimized for high-ingestion, low-latency time-series queries — and OneLake availability bridges to the lakehouse for long-term storage.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Eventstream (Fabric's event ingestion service) captures the 100K events/second stream and routes to a KQL database. KQL databases are optimized for time-series and log analytics with sub-second query response on billions of rows. The 7-day hot cache keeps recent data in SSD/memory for fast queries. OneLake availability automatically makes KQL data queryable from the lakehouse (as Delta tables) without manual export — enabling long-term historical analysis via Spark or SQL endpoint. Power BI streaming datasets cannot handle 100K events/second.

ul.li: KQL databases in Fabric support up to millions of events/second ingestion with columnar storage optimized for time-series.
Hot cache policy (set in days) determines how much data stays on fast storage vs. cold storage.
OneLake availability creates a mirrored Delta table — queryable via SQL endpoint and Spark without data copying overhead.
KQL geo-spatial functions (geo_point_in_polygon, geo_distance_point_to_line) enable route deviation detection natively.

question.title: Data Pipeline Monitoring
question.scenario: A data platform team runs 200 data pipelines in Fabric that execute throughout the day. They need: alerting when pipelines fail, SLA tracking (pipelines must complete within defined time windows), historical success/failure trends for capacity planning, and the ability to automatically retry failed pipelines with exponential backoff. Currently, failures go unnoticed until business users report missing data.
question.question-text: Which monitoring and reliability approach provides comprehensive pipeline observability?

choices.choice: Check pipeline run history manually in the Fabric portal each morning
Email notifications configured in each pipeline's success/failure paths only
Azure Monitor integration with Log Analytics workspace and custom Kusto queries

Data Pipeline monitoring with Fabric Monitoring Hub, alert rules on pipeline failures, retry policies with exponential backoff configured in pipeline activities, and Power BI dashboard on pipeline run metadata

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric's native monitoring capabilities combined with built-in retry policies provide the full observability stack.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric Monitoring Hub provides a centralized view of all pipeline runs across workspaces with status, duration, and error details. Alert rules trigger notifications (email, Teams) on pipeline failure events. Retry policies configured at the activity level support exponential backoff (e.g., retry 3 times with 10/20/40 minute intervals). Pipeline run metadata can be queried programmatically via REST API and visualized in a Power BI dashboard showing trends, SLA compliance (duration vs. target), and failure patterns for capacity planning.

ul.li: Monitoring Hub shows: item type, status, start time, duration, submitted by, and workspace — across all Fabric items.
Pipeline retry policies: configurable max retry count, interval in seconds, and backoff multiplier (exponential).
Fabric REST APIs (Items API, Pipeline API) enable programmatic access to run history for custom dashboards.
Data Activator (Reflex) can trigger alerts based on data conditions in addition to pipeline execution status.

question.title: Lakehouse vs Warehouse Selection
question.scenario: A company is deciding between a Fabric Lakehouse and a Fabric Warehouse for their new analytics platform. Their requirements include: support for semi-structured data (JSON, Avro), ability to use both Spark and T-SQL for processing, compatibility with existing Power BI semantic models, open data format for portability, and ACID transactions for reliable data updates.
question.question-text: Which Fabric item best meets all these requirements?

choices.choice: Fabric Warehouse — provides T-SQL, Power BI integration, and ACID transactions
External Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 with direct Power BI connection
Both a Lakehouse and Warehouse with data movement between them
Fabric Lakehouse — supports semi-structured data, Spark and T-SQL (via SQL endpoint), Delta format (open/portable), ACID transactions, and Power BI connectivity

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Which Fabric item natively supports ALL listed requirements: semi-structured data, dual engines (Spark + SQL), open format, and ACID?

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Fabric Lakehouse satisfies all requirements: the Files section stores semi-structured data (JSON, Avro, Parquet), Spark notebooks process data with full PySpark/Scala support, the auto-generated SQL analytics endpoint provides T-SQL access, Delta Lake format is open (Apache-licensed) for portability, Delta provides ACID transactions, and the default semantic model connects directly to Power BI. The Warehouse would require data to already be structured and does not natively support Spark processing or semi-structured file storage.

ul.li: Lakehouse has two sections: Tables (managed Delta tables) and Files (unstructured/semi-structured storage).
The SQL analytics endpoint is read-only — writes must happen through Spark or Data Pipeline.
Delta Lake is an open-source project (Linux Foundation) ensuring no vendor lock-in for data format.
Fabric Warehouse provides full DML (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) via T-SQL — choose it when T-SQL write access is the primary need.

question.title: Spark Notebook Best Practices
question.scenario: A data engineer writes a Spark notebook that reads 500GB of raw data from the lakehouse Files section, performs complex transformations (window functions, UDFs, multiple joins), and writes results to a managed Delta table. The notebook takes 3 hours to complete and frequently fails with OutOfMemory errors at the join stage. The engineer is using a default Spark session with no custom configuration.
question.question-text: Which combination of techniques will most effectively reduce execution time and eliminate OOM errors?

choices.choice: Switch to a larger Spark pool with more memory per executor
Convert all transformations to SQL using spark.sql() instead of DataFrame API
Optimize the join with broadcast hints for small tables, repartition data before the join stage, use Delta table partitioning on the write, and enable adaptive query execution (AQE)
Split the notebook into 10 smaller notebooks running sequentially

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: OOM during joins typically means data skew or large shuffle — broadcast, repartition, and AQE address these root causes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Broadcast hints join small dimension tables (<500MB) without shuffle — eliminating OOM risk for those joins. Repartitioning before large joins distributes data evenly across executors, preventing single-partition memory pressure. AQE (Adaptive Query Execution) dynamically adjusts partition counts, handles skew with skew join optimization, and coalesces small partitions — addressing the most common causes of OOM. Delta table partitioning on write (by date or key column) optimizes downstream read performance.

ul.li: Broadcast threshold default in Spark is 10MB — increase with spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold for tables up to 500MB.
AQE features: coalesce post-shuffle partitions, skew join handling, and dynamic join strategy selection — enable with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=true.
Repartition by join key before joining ensures co-located data — repartition(200, "join_key") is often optimal.
UDFs prevent Catalyst optimization — consider replacing with native Spark functions where possible for better performance.

question.title: DirectLake Mode
question.scenario: A company has a 50GB semantic model currently in Import mode that refreshes every 4 hours. Business users complain about stale data between refreshes. The data lives in a Fabric lakehouse Delta table that receives continuous updates throughout the day. The team wants near-real-time data freshness in Power BI reports without the performance degradation typically associated with DirectQuery.
question.question-text: Which semantic model storage mode provides near-real-time freshness with Import-like performance?

choices.choice: DirectQuery mode connecting to the lakehouse SQL endpoint
Composite model with Import for historical data and DirectQuery for recent data
Import mode with incremental refresh set to 15-minute intervals
DirectLake mode — reads Delta Parquet files directly from OneLake with in-memory columnar engine performance

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: DirectLake is unique to Fabric — it reads directly from Delta files but processes them through the VertiPaq engine for Import-like speed.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: DirectLake mode reads Parquet files from Delta tables in OneLake directly into the VertiPaq columnar engine — no data copy or scheduled refresh needed. When the underlying Delta table is updated, DirectLake automatically detects the new files and loads them on the next query (or within a short framing interval). This provides near-real-time freshness (minutes, not hours) with the performance of Import mode (in-memory columnar). Unlike DirectQuery, it does not generate queries against a SQL engine for every report interaction.

ul.li: DirectLake requires data in Fabric lakehouse or warehouse Delta tables — external data sources are not supported.
Framing: DirectLake periodically checks for new Delta files; explicit framing can be triggered via XMLA endpoint.
Fallback: if a DAX query cannot be served from loaded Parquet segments, DirectLake falls back to DirectQuery automatically.
Guardrails exist: max rows per table, max model size — exceeding these causes fallback to DirectQuery behavior.

question.title: Notebook Visualization and Sharing
question.scenario: A data scientist builds an exploratory analysis in a Fabric Spark notebook. The analysis includes data profiling, statistical summaries, correlation matrices, and predictive model results. They need to share interactive findings with business stakeholders who do not have Fabric workspace access and are not technical users. The stakeholders should be able to filter and interact with the visualizations without running any code.
question.question-text: Which approach best shares interactive notebook findings with non-technical stakeholders?

choices.choice: Give stakeholders Viewer role in the workspace to view notebook outputs
Export notebook results to a Power BI report using the notebook's built-in chart visualizations, then share the report via Power BI app or embed in Teams
Schedule the notebook to email HTML outputs to stakeholders daily
Convert notebook outputs to PDF and distribute via email

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Power BI reports provide interactive visualizations that non-technical users can filter and explore — and can be shared widely without Fabric access.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Writing notebook analysis results to a lakehouse table, then building a Power BI report on that data, provides the interactive experience stakeholders need (filters, slicers, drill-through) without code exposure. Power BI apps and Teams embedding share reports with users who have no Fabric workspace access. Notebook visualizations require workspace access and code execution context — not suitable for non-technical audiences. This pattern separates the analytical computation (notebook) from the presentation layer (Power BI).

ul.li: Fabric notebooks support inline visualizations (matplotlib, plotly, seaborn) but these require workspace access to view.
Power BI reports connected to lakehouse tables via DirectLake provide live data without scheduled refresh.
Power BI Apps provide a curated, read-only experience with pre-configured navigation — ideal for business users.
Teams embedding allows stakeholders to interact with reports without leaving their collaboration tool.

question.title: Data Lineage and Impact Analysis
question.scenario: A data engineer needs to modify the schema of a silver-layer Delta table (renaming a column and changing its data type). Before making the change, they need to understand all downstream dependencies: which gold-layer tables read from this table, which semantic models reference these columns, which Power BI reports will break, and which scheduled pipelines will fail. The lakehouse has 200 tables with complex interdependencies.
question.question-text: Which Fabric capability provides this end-to-end dependency and impact analysis?

choices.choice: Fabric lineage view showing upstream and downstream dependencies across items (tables, models, reports, pipelines) with column-level lineage in semantic models
Search through all notebook code manually for references to the table name
Query the Delta table transaction log for read operations from other tables
Power BI impact analysis for reports only, with manual pipeline review

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric provides built-in lineage visualization that traces data flow from source through transformation to consumption across all item types.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric lineage view (accessible from workspace settings and individual items) shows the complete dependency graph: which items read from and write to each other. For a lakehouse table, it shows downstream dependencies including other tables that read from it (via notebooks/pipelines), semantic models that reference it, and Power BI reports built on those models. Column-level lineage in semantic models traces specific columns through relationships and measures. This enables impact analysis before schema changes — identifying exactly what will break.

ul.li: Lineage view supports: Lakehouses, Warehouses, Pipelines, Dataflows, Notebooks, Semantic Models, Reports, and Dashboards.
Column-level lineage tracks which source columns map to which semantic model columns through transformations.
Impact analysis in Power BI workspace shows report and dashboard counts affected by dataset schema changes.
Purview integration extends lineage beyond Fabric to external data sources (Azure SQL, Synapse, on-premises).

question.title: Shortcut Strategy
question.scenario: A company has existing data in Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 (2PB) and AWS S3 (500TB) that they cannot move to Fabric OneLake due to egress costs and data residency requirements. They need this external data to be queryable alongside Fabric-native lakehouse data using the same tools (Spark, SQL endpoint, Power BI). No data duplication is acceptable.
question.question-text: Which Fabric feature enables querying external data without duplication or data movement?

choices.choice: OneLake shortcuts pointing to ADLS Gen2 and S3 locations — queryable as native lakehouse tables without data movement
Use Data Pipeline Copy Activity to replicate external data into the lakehouse on a schedule
Mount external storage as a Spark file system (abfss://) and query directly without any Fabric integration
Create a Fabric Warehouse with external tables referencing the remote storage

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Shortcuts create virtual references in OneLake to external storage — data appears as lakehouse tables without physical movement.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: OneLake shortcuts create virtual pointers to data in ADLS Gen2 and AWS S3. The external data appears in the lakehouse Tables section alongside native Delta tables — queryable via Spark notebooks, SQL analytics endpoint, and Power BI reports without any data copying. Reads go directly to the source storage. For Delta-formatted external data, full ACID semantics are preserved. For Parquet/CSV external data, read-only access is provided. This satisfies the zero-duplication and data residency requirements while enabling unified analytics.

ul.li: Shortcuts support: other OneLake locations, ADLS Gen2, AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Dataverse.
Authentication: ADLS shortcuts use organizational identity or service principal; S3 uses access key or IAM role.
Performance consideration: queries on shortcut data traverse the network to source storage — latency depends on source location.
Shortcuts respect source permissions — Fabric users must be authorized at both the Fabric and source storage level.

question.title: Incremental Data Loading
question.scenario: A data pipeline loads transactional data from an operational SQL database into a lakehouse Delta table. The source table has 500 million rows and grows by 2 million rows daily. Currently, the pipeline does a full reload daily (6 hours). The team needs to reduce this to incremental loads that capture only new and modified records, with the ability to handle both inserts and updates (records can be modified up to 7 days after creation).
question.question-text: Which incremental loading pattern efficiently captures inserts and updates from the source?

choices.choice: CDC (Change Data Capture) from the source database to capture insert/update/delete events, with Delta MERGE to apply changes to the lakehouse table
Full reload with table truncate and reload approach optimized with parallel threads
Query only records from the last 24 hours based on created_date column and append to the Delta table
Compare source and target tables row-by-row to find differences and apply updates

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: CDC captures the exact changes (inserts, updates, deletes) at the source — Delta MERGE applies them idempotently to the target.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: CDC (Change Data Capture) on the source SQL database captures every insert, update, and delete as change events with timestamps. The Fabric pipeline reads only new CDC records since the last watermark. Delta MERGE (MERGE INTO target USING changes ON key WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT) applies these changes idempotently to the lakehouse table. This handles both inserts and updates (including modifications up to 7 days later) without full table scans of either source or target.

ul.li: SQL Server CDC uses the transaction log to capture changes — minimal impact on source performance.
Delta MERGE is atomic — all changes succeed or none do (ACID transaction on the target table).
Watermark pattern: store the last processed CDC LSN/timestamp; next run reads only changes after that point.
For Azure SQL: Use Data Pipeline with CDC-enabled source and incremental watermark tracking in pipeline variables.

question.title: Row-Level Security Implementation
question.scenario: A multinational corporation has a single semantic model for sales reporting. Regional sales managers should only see data for their own region (Americas, EMEA, APAC). The VP of Sales should see all regions. The security must be dynamic — when a new manager is hired, access should be granted without modifying the semantic model. There are 500 users across the organization who access these reports.
question.question-text: Which RLS implementation provides dynamic, maintenance-free security that scales to 500 users?

choices.choice: Dynamic RLS using USERPRINCIPALNAME() matched against a security table that maps users to regions, with a role for the VP that has no filter (sees all data)
Create separate reports per region with workspace-level access control
Static RLS with a separate role per region and manually assign users to roles
Use Power BI Row-Level Security with hardcoded email addresses in DAX filter expressions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Dynamic RLS uses a security mapping table — no model changes needed when users change, just update the table.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Dynamic RLS creates a single role with a DAX filter expression that references a security table: FILTER(Regions, CONTAINS(SecurityTable, SecurityTable[UserPrincipalName], USERPRINCIPALNAME(), SecurityTable[Region], Regions[Region])). When new managers join, their mapping is added to the security table (which can be a lakehouse table refreshed automatically). The VP role has no DAX filter — they see all data. This scales to any number of users without model modification. Only the security table needs maintenance.

ul.li: USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the authenticated user's email — works in Power BI Service, embedded, and Teams.
Security table can live in the lakehouse and sync from Active Directory or HR system automatically.
Performance: RLS filters are applied at query time — ensure the security table has a relationship to the model for efficient filtering.
Testing: "View as" in Power BI Service allows admins to test RLS as specific users before deployment.

question.title: Cross-Workspace Analytics
question.scenario: A company has domain-specific workspaces (Sales, Marketing, Finance, Operations) each with their own lakehouses. The executive team needs a unified analytics layer that combines data from all domains without moving data between workspaces. For example, a report showing marketing campaign ROI needs data from both the Marketing lakehouse (campaign metrics) and the Sales lakehouse (revenue attribution). Domain teams must retain ownership of their data.
question.question-text: Which Fabric pattern enables cross-domain analytics while preserving domain data ownership?

choices.choice: Copy all data into a single centralized lakehouse owned by a BI team
Use DirectQuery semantic models connecting to each domain's SQL endpoint independently
Create an analytics workspace with a lakehouse that uses OneLake shortcuts to each domain workspace's lakehouse tables, enabling unified queries without data movement
Schedule nightly data exports from each domain to a shared file location

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Shortcuts within OneLake can reference other workspaces' lakehouses — creating a virtual unified view without data duplication.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: An analytics workspace with its own lakehouse creates OneLake shortcuts pointing to tables in each domain workspace. This creates a unified query surface — Spark notebooks or the SQL endpoint can join tables across domains as if they were local. No data is copied (shortcuts are virtual references). Domain teams retain full ownership and control of their source lakehouses. The analytics workspace only needs read access (via workspace roles) to the source workspaces. This is the Fabric implementation of a data mesh access layer.

ul.li: Internal OneLake shortcuts (within Fabric) have no egress costs — reads traverse the OneLake namespace directly.
Permissions: the shortcut consumer needs at least Viewer role in the source workspace to access the data.
SQL endpoint cross-database queries: FROM [other_lakehouse].[dbo].[table] enables joins across lakehouses in Spark SQL.
This pattern aligns with data mesh principles: domain ownership + centralized discovery/governance + self-serve access.

question.title: Governance and Compliance
question.scenario: A financial services company using Fabric must comply with SOX regulations requiring: data classification (identifying PII and financial data), access audit trails (who accessed what data and when), data retention policies (7-year minimum for financial records), and prevention of unauthorized data sharing outside the organization. They have 1,000 users across 50 workspaces.
question.question-text: Which combination of Fabric governance features addresses these compliance requirements?

choices.choice: Manual data classification spreadsheets and quarterly access reviews

Microsoft Purview for data classification and sensitivity labels, Fabric audit logs for access tracking, workspace-level retention policies, and sensitivity label-based DLP policies preventing external sharing of labeled data
Azure Policy applied to the Fabric tenant for all governance requirements
Workspace admin roles with custom scripts to track data access from pipeline logs

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Microsoft Purview integrates with Fabric for classification, and sensitivity labels drive DLP policies — audit logs provide the access trail.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Microsoft Purview scans Fabric items and automatically classifies sensitive data (PII, financial data) using built-in and custom classifiers. Sensitivity labels (Confidential, Highly Confidential) applied to Fabric items flow through to exports and sharing — DLP policies prevent sharing of labeled items externally. Fabric audit logs (via Microsoft 365 unified audit) record every data access event (who, what, when) for SOX compliance. Information protection policies enforce retention and prevent deletion of financial records within the retention period.

ul.li: Purview sensitivity labels in Fabric: applied to semantic models, reports, lakehouses — inherited downstream automatically.
Audit logs capture: report views, data exports, sharing events, admin actions — searchable in Microsoft 365 Compliance Center.
DLP policies for Fabric: detect and block sharing of items containing credit card numbers, SSNs, or custom patterns.
Retention labels applied via Purview prevent deletion of Fabric items until the retention period expires (legal hold capable).

question.title: Data Ingestion Patterns
question.scenario: A company receives data from multiple sources with different delivery patterns: hourly CSV files dropped to Azure Blob Storage (10GB/hour), real-time events from an Azure Event Hub (50,000 events/second), daily database extracts from SAP via OData API (200GB), and weekly Excel files uploaded by business analysts to a SharePoint folder. All data must land in the lakehouse for unified analytics.
question.question-text: Which combination of Fabric ingestion methods handles all four source patterns?

choices.choice: Use a single Data Pipeline with different activities scheduled at different frequencies for all sources
Dataflow Gen2 for all sources with Power Query connectors
Spark notebooks for all four sources with different schedules
OneLake shortcut for Blob Storage CSVs, Eventstream for Event Hub real-time data, Data Pipeline with Copy Activity for SAP OData, and Dataflow Gen2 for SharePoint Excel files

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Match each source pattern (batch files, streaming, API, small files) to the Fabric ingestion tool designed for that pattern.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: OneLake shortcuts to Blob Storage make CSV files immediately queryable without ingestion latency or data copying (ideal for frequent batch files). Eventstream captures Event Hub events in real-time and routes to lakehouse or KQL database. Data Pipeline with Copy Activity handles the scheduled SAP OData extraction with pagination and error handling at 200GB scale. Dataflow Gen2 with Power Query Excel connector handles the low-volume SharePoint files with familiar transformation UI for business analyst self-service. Each tool is purpose-built for its source pattern.

ul.li: Blob Storage shortcuts: zero-copy, zero-latency — files are queryable immediately upon landing in source storage.
Eventstream supports: Event Hubs, IoT Hub, Custom App (SDK), and Kafka as sources with sub-second latency to destinations.
Copy Activity OData connector: supports pagination, $filter, $select, and OAuth2/basic authentication.
Dataflow Gen2 SharePoint connector: handles Excel, CSV, and JSON files from SharePoint Online with folder and file discovery.

question.title: Data Quality Framework
question.scenario: A healthcare data platform processes patient records that must meet strict data quality standards before being used in clinical reports. Requirements include: null checks on mandatory fields (patient_id, date_of_birth), referential integrity validation (diagnosis codes must exist in a reference table), range validation (age between 0 and 150, blood pressure within physiological limits), and freshness checks (data must not be older than 24 hours). Failed records must be quarantined for review, not dropped silently.
question.question-text: Which data quality implementation ensures validation, quarantine, and auditability in Fabric?

choices.choice: Spark notebook with validation logic that writes passing records to the gold table and failing records to a quarantine table with failure reasons, tracked via a data quality metrics table
Apply constraints on the Delta table schema to reject invalid data at write time
Power Query data profiling in Dataflow Gen2 with conditional column filters
SQL stored procedures on the warehouse SQL endpoint with CHECK constraints

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A validation notebook can apply complex rules (including referential integrity) and route records to either the target or quarantine table with full audit trails.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A Spark notebook reads staged records, applies validation rules (null checks, range validation, referential integrity joins against reference tables, freshness checks on timestamps), and classifies each record as pass or fail. Passing records are written to the gold Delta table. Failing records are written to a quarantine Delta table with columns for: failure reason, rule violated, timestamp, and source batch ID. A metrics table tracks pass/fail rates over time for monitoring. This provides full auditability — no records are silently dropped, and every failure is explained.

ul.li: Delta table constraints (CHECK constraints) only support simple column-level validation — not referential integrity or cross-table checks.
Quarantine pattern: quarantine table mirrors source schema plus: rule_id, failure_description, quarantine_timestamp, resolution_status.
Great Expectations library integrates with Spark for declarative rule definition — consider for large rule sets.
Data quality metrics (records processed, pass rate, failure categories) can feed a Power BI monitoring dashboard for the data steward.

question.title: Composite Model Design
question.scenario: A company's enterprise semantic model has become too large (200GB) for Import mode. Most tables are slowly-changing dimensions and historical facts that rarely change, but the sales transaction table (100GB) updates every 15 minutes. Analysts need fast report performance for dashboards that combine historical trends with current-day transactions. Moving entirely to DirectQuery would degrade interactive report performance unacceptably.
question.question-text: Which semantic model configuration balances freshness with performance for this mixed workload?

choices.choice: Composite model: DirectLake mode for the frequently-updated sales transaction table, Import mode for slowly-changing dimensions and historical facts
Full DirectQuery mode for all tables with aggressive caching at the report level
Import mode for all tables with 15-minute incremental refresh on the sales table
Separate models — one Import for history, one DirectQuery for real-time — with drillthrough between reports

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Composite models mix storage modes — use the fastest mode for each table based on its update frequency and query pattern.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A composite model uses DirectLake for the sales transaction table — providing near-real-time data (from the underlying Delta table updates) with VertiPaq-like query performance, no scheduled refresh needed. Import mode for dimensions and historical facts provides maximum query speed for the stable majority of the model. When reports combine both (e.g., current sales by product category), the engine handles the cross-mode joins transparently. This eliminates the 200GB Import refresh problem while maintaining interactive performance.

ul.li: Composite models in Fabric can mix: Import, DirectLake, and DirectQuery within a single model.
Cross-mode join performance: the engine materializes the DirectLake/DirectQuery side and joins in memory.
Import tables in composite models still need refresh — but only for the stable dimensions (small, infrequent).
Best practice: keep all dimensions in Import mode for filter performance; only transaction/fact tables need DirectLake for freshness.

question.title: Data Activator (Reflex)
question.scenario: A manufacturing operations team monitors production line metrics in a Power BI report. They need automated actions when specific conditions are met: send a Teams notification when defect rate exceeds 5%, pause the production pipeline in Fabric when input data quality drops below a threshold, and create a ServiceNow ticket when equipment temperature exceeds safe limits. Currently, operators manually watch dashboards 24/7.
question.question-text: Which Fabric feature automates actions based on data conditions without manual monitoring?

choices.choice: Scheduled Power BI report subscriptions with threshold alerts sent via email
Custom Python script running on a schedule checking metrics and sending alerts
Azure Logic Apps with scheduled queries against the lakehouse SQL endpoint
Data Activator (Reflex) with triggers monitoring data conditions and configured actions (Teams notifications, Power Automate flows for ServiceNow, and Fabric REST API calls for pipeline control)

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Data Activator monitors data conditions continuously and triggers actions automatically — replacing manual dashboard watching.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Data Activator (Reflex) in Fabric monitors data from multiple sources (Power BI visuals, Eventstream, Fabric items) and triggers actions when specified conditions are met. Triggers define the condition (defect_rate > 5%, temperature > threshold) and the action (Teams notification, email, Power Automate flow). Power Automate integration enables complex actions like creating ServiceNow tickets or calling Fabric REST APIs to pause pipelines. This provides 24/7 automated monitoring without human dashboard watching, reducing response time from hours to seconds.

ul.li: Data Activator connects to: Power BI report visuals (right-click > "Set alert"), Eventstream real-time data, and custom data via REST API.
Triggers support: threshold crossing, rate of change, pattern detection (sustained above X for Y minutes).
Actions: Email, Teams message, Power Automate flow (enabling any downstream action the flow platform supports).
Evaluation frequency is configurable — from every few seconds (Eventstream) to hourly (Power BI refresh-based).

question.title: Lakehouse Maintenance
question.scenario: A lakehouse has 500 Delta tables that have been in production for 6 months. Performance has degraded significantly: queries take 3x longer than initial benchmarks. Investigation reveals: tables have thousands of small files (1-10MB each) from frequent micro-batch writes, Delta transaction logs have grown large (10,000+ entries per table without checkpoints), and deleted/updated data files have not been cleaned up (vacuum never run), consuming 2x the expected storage.
question.question-text: Which maintenance strategy restores performance and reduces storage waste?

choices.choice: Drop and recreate all tables from source data
Increase Spark executor count to brute-force through the small files

Schedule OPTIMIZE (bin compaction) for all tables, run VACUUM to remove obsolete files, and configure checkpoint interval to control log growth — implemented as a maintenance notebook on a nightly schedule
Migrate all tables to Parquet format without Delta Lake overhead

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Delta tables require periodic maintenance: OPTIMIZE compacts files, VACUUM removes old files, and checkpointing controls log size.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: OPTIMIZE compacts thousands of small files into fewer, larger files (target ~1GB) — dramatically reducing the number of file reads per query. VACUUM removes files no longer referenced by the Delta log (from previous UPDATE/DELETE/MERGE operations), reclaiming the 2x storage overhead. Delta automatically creates checkpoints every 10 commits by default, but tables with very frequent micro-batch writes may benefit from explicit checkpointing configuration. Scheduling these as a nightly maintenance notebook ensures ongoing performance without manual intervention.

ul.li: OPTIMIZE in Fabric: compacts files within each partition, supports ZORDER for co-location optimization.
VACUUM default retention: 7 days (168 hours). Never set below the longest-running query duration to avoid breaking active reads.
Delta checkpoints: Parquet file summarizing the table state, avoiding log replay from the beginning. Created every 10 commits by default.
Fabric Lakehouse tables have automatic optimization enabled by default for new tables — but existing tables from before the feature need manual maintenance.

question.title: Mirroring for Operational Analytics
question.scenario: A company uses Azure SQL Database as their primary transactional system. Business analysts need near-real-time analytics on operational data without impacting transaction processing. The current approach — nightly ETL to the lakehouse — means analysts work with stale data. They need continuous replication with minimal latency and zero impact on the source database performance.
question.question-text: Which Fabric feature provides continuous, low-impact replication from Azure SQL to the lakehouse?

choices.choice: Fabric Mirroring for Azure SQL Database — continuous change replication to OneLake Delta tables with near-real-time latency and no source performance impact
Data Pipeline with Copy Activity scheduled every 5 minutes for incremental loads
Azure SQL Database linked service with DirectQuery from Power BI
Azure Data Factory Change Data Capture connector writing to a Fabric lakehouse

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric Mirroring provides continuous, change-based replication from operational databases to OneLake without ETL pipelines.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric Mirroring creates a continuously synchronized copy of Azure SQL Database tables as Delta tables in OneLake. It uses change feed technology to capture only changed rows (inserts, updates, deletes) with near-real-time latency (seconds to minutes). The replication is read-only from the source — no agents installed, no load on the transaction processing. The mirrored data is immediately queryable via SQL endpoint, Spark, and Power BI DirectLake mode, providing analysts with fresh operational data without impacting the source system.

ul.li: Mirroring supports: Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, Snowflake, Azure SQL Managed Instance, and more sources.
Replication latency: typically seconds to a few minutes depending on change volume and source type.
Zero impact on source: uses read-only change tracking/CDC mechanisms without installing agents or triggers.
Mirrored tables appear in a Mirrored Database item in Fabric — queryable identically to native lakehouse tables.

question.title: Slowly Changing Dimensions
question.scenario: A retail company's customer dimension table needs to handle customer address changes. When a customer moves, the business requires: the current address for shipping and billing (Type 1 — overwrite), the history of all addresses for marketing analytics (Type 2 — new row), and the original address at time of first purchase preserved (Type 3 — additional column). The table has 10 million customers with an average of 3 address changes per customer over 5 years.
question.question-text: Which SCD implementation in Fabric handles all three requirements simultaneously?

choices.choice: Single Type 2 table with is_current flag, effective_date/end_date columns, and an additional original_address column for the first-ever record — maintained via Delta MERGE with SCD logic in a Spark notebook
Three separate tables: one Type 1 (current only), one Type 2 (full history), and one Type 3 (original + current)
Update-in-place for all changes and rely on Delta time travel to query historical states
Append-only table with no distinction between current and historical records

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: A combined SCD approach in a single table uses Type 2 structure (history rows) with a current flag and additional columns for Type 3 attributes.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A single table with Type 2 structure (surrogate key, effective_date, end_date, is_current flag) preserves full address history. The is_current = true row always has the latest address (satisfying Type 1 queries via a simple filter). An original_address column on every row stores the first-ever address (Type 3). Delta MERGE in a Spark notebook handles the logic: when an address change arrives, expire the current row (set end_date, is_current=false), insert a new row with the new address (is_current=true), and copy original_address from the expired row. This unified approach avoids data duplication across multiple tables.

ul.li: Delta MERGE supports complex WHEN MATCHED / WHEN NOT MATCHED logic needed for SCD Type 2 operations.
Surrogate keys (monotonically_increasing_id or hash-based) enable joining facts to the correct dimension version.
Delta time travel is NOT a substitute for SCD2 — it has a retention limit and doesn't preserve business-meaningful versioning.
Performance tip: partition the dimension by is_current for fast current-state queries (most queries only need current rows).

question.title: Large Semantic Model Optimization
question.scenario: A retail company's semantic model has grown to 80GB with 3 billion rows in the fact table. Report page load times have increased to 30 seconds. Analysis shows: the fact table stores daily granularity data from 10 years ago but reports only drill to daily for the last 2 years, 50% of columns in the fact table are never used in any report, and text columns with high cardinality (product descriptions, 500K unique values) are included but only used for tooltips.
question.question-text: Which optimization combination will most reduce model size and improve report performance?

choices.choice: Upgrade to a larger Fabric capacity for more processing power
Enable automatic aggregations on the fact table and let the engine handle optimization
Switch the entire model to DirectQuery to eliminate model size concerns
Aggregate older data to monthly granularity (aggregation table), remove unused columns, and move high-cardinality text to a separate detail table with drill-through access

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Reduce what's in the model: aggregate old data, remove unused columns, and isolate high-cardinality text — all directly reduce model size.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Aggregating 8 years of daily data to monthly reduces those rows by ~30x (from 2.9B rows to ~100M for old data + keeping 730 days at daily = ~730M rows — total model drops significantly). Removing the 50% unused columns immediately halves the remaining model's column storage. Moving high-cardinality text (500K unique values) to a drill-through detail table means the main model's dictionary encoding is not bloated by those strings. Combined, these optimizations can reduce the model from 80GB to under 10GB while preserving all report functionality through aggregation awareness and drill-through patterns.

ul.li: VertiPaq compression is dictionary-based — high cardinality text columns compress poorly and bloat memory.
User-defined aggregation tables with the "Manage aggregations" feature in Power BI route queries to the appropriate granularity automatically.
DAX Studio or Tabular Editor VertiPaq Analyzer identifies which columns consume the most memory for targeted optimization.
Rule of thumb: every column removed reduces model size proportionally — a 50-column fact table cut to 25 columns halves that table's storage.

question.title: Spark vs SQL Endpoint Selection
question.scenario: A data team needs to perform different types of analyses on lakehouse data: exploratory data science with statistical libraries (scipy, sklearn), complex data transformations with window functions and pivot operations, scheduled ETL producing derived tables, and ad-hoc business reporting queries. Team members have varied backgrounds — data scientists prefer Python, data engineers prefer SQL, and business analysts prefer drag-and-drop interfaces.
question.question-text: Which Fabric compute assignment provides optimal tool-to-task matching for this diverse team?

choices.choice: Spark notebooks for everything — SQL users can use spark.sql()
SQL analytics endpoint for everything — data scientists can use SQL-based ML
Separate instances of each tool per team member regardless of task type
Spark notebooks for data science and complex ETL, SQL analytics endpoint for ad-hoc business queries and simple reporting, Dataflow Gen2 for business analyst self-service transformations

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Match compute to the task and user skill set — each Fabric engine excels at different workloads.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Spark notebooks are ideal for data science (Python with scipy, sklearn, pandas) and complex ETL (distributed processing, UDFs, streaming). The SQL analytics endpoint provides T-SQL for ad-hoc queries and business reporting — familiar to analysts using SSMS or Azure Data Studio, with no Spark session startup time. Dataflow Gen2's Power Query interface provides drag-and-drop transformation for business analysts without code. This assignment leverages each engine's strengths while respecting team skill sets — maximizing productivity across all user personas.

ul.li: Spark session startup takes 30-60 seconds — SQL endpoint queries are instant (always-on engine).
SQL endpoint is read-only for lakehouse tables — writes require Spark, Pipeline, or Dataflow.
Dataflow Gen2 Power Query supports 300+ connectors with no-code transformation for citizen data engineers.
All three engines read the same Delta tables — no data copying needed when switching between tools.

question.title: Cost Management
question.scenario: A company's Fabric capacity costs are growing 30% month-over-month. The platform team needs to: identify which workspaces and workloads consume the most capacity units (CUs), detect inefficient patterns (runaway Spark jobs, unoptimized queries), implement showback/chargeback to business units based on consumption, and set guardrails to prevent any single team from exhausting shared capacity.
question.question-text: Which approach provides cost visibility, optimization, and governance for Fabric capacity?

choices.choice: Review the monthly Azure invoice for total Fabric spend without workspace breakdown
Purchase the largest possible capacity to avoid throttling without cost optimization
Disable Fabric features for teams that consume too many resources without analysis

Fabric Capacity Metrics app for consumption analysis by workspace and workload type, admin APIs for programmatic cost allocation, workspace-specific capacity assignment for high-consumption teams, and Spark pool size limits per workspace

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The Capacity Metrics app provides consumption breakdown — combine with admin APIs and workspace isolation for governance.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Fabric Capacity Metrics app (installable from AppSource) provides detailed breakdowns: CU consumption by workspace, item type (Spark, SQL, Dataflow, Power BI), user, and time period — enabling identification of top consumers and inefficient patterns. Admin REST APIs expose the same data programmatically for building chargeback reports allocated to business units. Assigning high-consumption teams to dedicated capacities prevents them from impacting others. Spark pool configuration limits (max nodes, timeout) per workspace prevent runaway jobs.

ul.li: Capacity Metrics app shows: interactive vs. background CU consumption, throttling events, and overages over 24-hour smoothing periods.
CU consumption varies by workload: Spark jobs consume more CUs than SQL queries for the same data volume.
Admin APIs (Microsoft.Fabric/capacities/metrics) enable custom Power BI reports for executive cost dashboards.
Capacity reservation: F2 through F2048 SKUs with per-second billing — right-sizing the SKU is the primary cost lever.

question.title: Multi-Format Data Handling
question.scenario: A data lake migration brings data in multiple formats: legacy Parquet files (partitioned by year/month/day), CSV files with inconsistent schemas (columns vary across files), JSON files with deeply nested structures (5 levels deep), and Avro files from Kafka topics. All must be consolidated into managed Delta tables in the lakehouse with a consistent schema. Some source files have no headers, incorrect data types, and encoding issues (UTF-8 and Latin-1 mixed).
question.question-text: Which Spark approach handles multi-format ingestion with schema inconsistencies robustly?

choices.choice: Use Auto Loader (Auto Schema) for all file types and let Spark infer everything automatically

Format-specific readers with explicit schema definitions, schema evolution via mergeSchema, encoding specification, and corrupt record handling using PERMISSIVE mode with a rescue column for malformed data
Convert all files to CSV first, then process uniformly as CSV
Use Dataflow Gen2 Power Query for all file formats with automatic type detection

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Explicit schemas prevent type inference errors, PERMISSIVE mode captures malformed records instead of failing, and encoding options handle character set mismatches.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Format-specific readers (spark.read.parquet, .csv, .json, .format("avro")) with explicitly defined schemas (using StructType) prevent incorrect type inference that plagues inconsistent CSVs. PERMISSIVE mode with columnNameOfCorruptRecord captures malformed rows in a rescue column instead of silently dropping them or failing the job. The .option("encoding", "latin1") handles non-UTF-8 files. Schema evolution via mergeSchema on the Delta write handles columns varying across files. This approach is robust, auditable (corrupt records are preserved), and handles all listed edge cases.

ul.li: PERMISSIVE mode: puts corrupt records in _corrupt_record column; DROPMALFORMED silently drops them; FAILFAST aborts the job.
Explicit schema avoids costly schema inference pass (which reads all files) and prevents type misdetection (e.g., "001" as integer 1).
JSON schema_of_json() function can generate StructType from a sample record for deeply nested structures.
Delta mergeSchema adds new columns from source files that have extra columns — existing columns with different types require explicit casting.

question.title: Parameterized Pipelines
question.scenario: A data engineering team manages 30 source systems that follow the same ingestion pattern: extract from source, land in bronze, transform to silver, load to gold. Writing 30 separate pipelines is unmaintainable. They need a single parameterized pipeline that accepts: source connection string, source table name, bronze/silver/gold destination paths, transformation logic (column mappings vary per source), and scheduling frequency. Changes to the shared pipeline should propagate to all sources.
question.question-text: Which Fabric pipeline design pattern provides maintainable, reusable ingestion at scale?

choices.choice: 30 individual pipelines with copy-pasted activities and manual synchronization of changes

A metadata-driven pipeline: master pipeline reads configuration from a metadata table (source, destination, mappings, schedule), loops through entries with ForEach activity, and calls a shared child pipeline template with parameters for each source
A single massive pipeline with 30 branches using Switch activity on source name
Spark notebook that reads all 30 sources sequentially in a single job

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Metadata-driven architecture: store source configuration in a table, loop through it, and call a parameterized template pipeline for each entry.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A metadata-driven architecture separates configuration from logic. A metadata table (in the lakehouse or Dataverse) stores: source_connection, source_table, bronze_path, silver_path, gold_path, column_mappings (JSON), schedule, and enabled flag. The master pipeline reads this table with a Lookup activity, then ForEach iterates through entries, calling an Execute Pipeline activity that invokes the shared child pipeline with parameters. Adding a new source means adding a row to the metadata table — zero pipeline changes. Modifying the shared template propagates to all 30 sources immediately.

ul.li: ForEach supports sequential and parallel execution (batch count) — control parallelism based on source system capacity.
Dynamic content expressions: @item().source_table resolves metadata values into activity parameters at runtime.
Column mappings as JSON in metadata enable dynamic Copy Activity schema mapping without pipeline modification.
Error handling: each child pipeline execution is independent — one source failure doesn't block others (with appropriate error settings).

question.title: Power BI Report Performance
question.scenario: A Power BI report connected to a DirectLake semantic model loads slowly (12 seconds for the main page). The page has 15 visuals, including a table with 500,000 rows (scrollable), 3 slicers on high-cardinality columns (1 million unique values each), 5 card visuals with complex DAX measures using CALCULATE with multiple filters, and a map visual plotting 100,000 locations. The report serves 500 concurrent users.
question.question-text: Which combination of optimizations will most reduce page load time?

choices.choice: Switch to DirectQuery mode to reduce memory pressure from concurrent users
Add more Premium capacity to handle 500 concurrent users

Limit table visual to top 100 rows with drill-through for detail, replace high-cardinality slicers with dropdown search or hierarchy filters, simplify DAX measures using variables, and replace the map with a pre-aggregated regional summary visual
Enable automatic page refresh every 30 seconds to keep the cache warm

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Report performance is driven by: number of rows rendered, slicer cardinality, DAX complexity, and visual rendering cost — optimize each.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Limiting the table to top 100 rows eliminates rendering 500K DOM elements (the biggest performance killer in reports). Replacing high-cardinality slicers (1M values each) with search-enabled dropdowns prevents loading all values into the filter pane. DAX variables (VAR) prevent redundant CALCULATE evaluations — each variable is evaluated once and reused. Replacing the 100K-point map with a regional summary reduces both query and rendering time dramatically. These changes target the specific bottlenecks identified in the scenario.

ul.li: Table visuals rendering 500K+ rows generate massive DAX queries and DOM elements — Top N filter or pagination is essential.
Slicer performance: each slicer queries DISTINCT values at page load — 1M values * 3 slicers = 3M values loaded before any interaction.
DAX VAR pattern: VAR Sales = [Total Sales] RETURN DIVIDE(Sales, [Target]) evaluates Sales once vs. 2x without VAR.
Performance Analyzer in Power BI Desktop shows per-visual query time and rendering time — use it to identify which visual to fix first.

question.title: Git Integration for Fabric
question.scenario: A data platform team of 12 engineers works on the same Fabric workspace. They need: version control for notebooks, pipelines, and semantic model definitions, the ability to work on changes without affecting production, code review before changes go live, and rollback capability when deployments cause issues. Currently, any change made by one engineer immediately affects all users of the workspace.
question.question-text: Which Fabric development workflow provides version control, isolation, and safe deployment?

choices.choice: Each engineer works in a personal copy of the workspace with manual export/import of items

Fabric Git integration with Azure DevOps or GitHub: connect workspace to a repo, engineers work in feature branches synced to personal dev workspaces, pull requests for review, and main branch auto-syncs to production workspace via deployment pipeline
Use file versioning by saving notebooks with date suffixes (notebook_v1, notebook_v2)
Restrict edit access to a single engineer who manually applies changes from others

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric Git integration connects workspaces to Git repos — enabling branching, pull requests, and CI/CD for Fabric items.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric Git integration connects a workspace to a Git repository (Azure DevOps or GitHub). Engineers create feature branches and work in personal development workspaces synced to their branch — changes are isolated from production. When ready, they create pull requests for code review by peers. After merge to main, deployment pipelines promote changes from development to test to production workspaces. Rollback is a simple git revert + resync. All Fabric item definitions (notebooks, pipelines, semantic models, reports) are stored as code in the repo.

ul.li: Supported items for Git: Notebooks, Pipelines, Semantic Models, Reports, Lakehouses (metadata only — data stays in OneLake).
Conflict resolution: if two engineers modify the same item, Git merge conflict resolution applies at the definition level.
Deployment pipelines: Dev > Test > Prod stages with configurable deployment rules and parameter overrides per stage.
Limitation: Data in lakehouses is NOT version-controlled — only the item definitions (schema, configuration) are in Git.

question.title: Disaster Recovery for Fabric
question.scenario: A company runs mission-critical analytics in Fabric with an RPO of 1 hour and RTO of 4 hours. Their Fabric tenant is in the East US region. They need to survive a complete region failure and resume analytics operations in another region within the RTO. The data includes: 50TB in lakehouse Delta tables, 100 semantic models, 500 reports, and 200 data pipelines.
question.question-text: Which disaster recovery strategy meets the RPO/RTO requirements for Fabric?

choices.choice: Rely on Microsoft's built-in Fabric high availability within the region (no cross-region DR)
Manual export of all items weekly and store in a separate Azure region
BCDR capacity with cross-region replication enabled for OneLake data, Git-based item definitions for rapid re-deployment in secondary region, and documented runbooks for workspace recreation
Real-time replication using Data Pipeline to a lakehouse in a secondary Fabric capacity in another region

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric BCDR features plus Git-stored definitions provide the data replication and item recovery needed for cross-region DR.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric's BCDR (Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery) capacity settings enable geo-redundant replication of OneLake data to a paired region — meeting the 1-hour RPO for data. Git integration stores all item definitions (notebooks, pipelines, reports, semantic models) in a repository — enabling rapid re-deployment to a new workspace in the secondary region within the 4-hour RTO. Documented runbooks specify the recovery sequence: provision secondary capacity, create workspace, sync from Git, verify data accessibility. This combination protects both data and configuration.

ul.li: Fabric BCDR replicates OneLake data to the Azure paired region with configurable RPO (GRS replication).
Git-stored definitions enable "infrastructure as code" recovery — workspace items can be recreated from the repo in minutes.
Semantic models, reports, and pipelines are definition files — relatively small, quick to deploy from Git.
Key limitation: Fabric DR is capacity-level — individual workspace DR requires Git + manual workspace setup in the secondary region.

question.title: Data Partitioning Strategy
question.scenario: A lakehouse stores 5 years of e-commerce transaction data (10 billion rows). Most queries filter by: date range (last 30/90/365 days), country (50 countries), and product_category (200 categories). The table is currently unpartitioned and query scans take 15 minutes. The team wants to add partitioning but is concerned about over-partitioning creating too many small files. Daily data volume is 50GB.
question.question-text: Which partitioning strategy optimizes query performance without creating small-file problems?

choices.choice: Partition by country and product_category for maximum predicate pushdown (50 * 200 = 10,000 partitions)
Partition by date (year/month) providing 60 partitions, with ZORDER on country and product_category within partitions for efficient filtering on all three predicates
Partition by day (1,825 daily partitions) for finest-grained date filtering
No partitioning — rely solely on ZORDER across all three filter columns

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Year/month partitioning gives manageable partition count, while ZORDER handles the other filter dimensions within each partition.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Partitioning by year/month creates ~60 partitions — each containing ~166GB of data with optimal file sizes. Date-range queries (most common pattern) skip entire partitions via partition pruning.
