ZORDER on country and product_category co-locates data within each monthly partition, enabling file-level data skipping for those predicates. This avoids the 10,000-partition explosion (country * category) which would create many small files (<10MB each) degrading both write and read performance. Daily partitioning at 50GB/day also works but creates 1,825 partitions — manageable but more metadata overhead.

ul.li: Rule of thumb: each partition should contain at least 1GB of data to avoid small-file overhead.
ZORDER interleaves column values in file-level min/max statistics — queries on z-ordered columns skip non-relevant files.
Over-partitioning (too many small files) causes: slow metadata operations, excessive file listing, and poor compression.
Combining partition pruning (date) + data skipping (ZORDER) typically achieves 95%+ data elimination for selective queries.

question.title: Error Handling in Pipelines
question.scenario: A critical data pipeline runs nightly and processes data from 5 independent sources. If one source fails (network timeout, schema change, source unavailable), the pipeline currently aborts entirely — blocking all 5 sources from loading. The team needs: independent processing per source (one failure doesn't block others), automatic retry with backoff for transient errors, alerting on permanent failures, and a summary log showing which sources succeeded and which failed with error details.
question.question-text: Which pipeline error handling design provides independent processing with comprehensive failure management?

choices.choice: Sequential activities with a single try-catch around the entire pipeline

ForEach activity (parallel) iterating over sources with retry policies on each Copy Activity, per-source error handling using If Condition on activity output, a Set Variable activity accumulating results, and a final notification activity summarizing successes and failures
Five separate pipelines triggered independently with no coordination or summary
A single Copy Activity with multiple sources and "continue on error" enabled

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: ForEach with per-iteration error handling provides independence — combined with result accumulation for a summary notification.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: ForEach with parallel execution processes all 5 sources independently — one failure doesn't block others. Within each iteration: Copy Activity has retry policy (count=3, interval=exponential backoff) handling transient errors automatically. If Condition checks the activity output status — on failure, captures error details into a variable array. After ForEach completes, a notification activity (email/Teams) sends a summary: which sources loaded successfully (with row counts) and which failed (with error messages). This provides resilience, automation, and observability in a single pipeline.

ul.li: ForEach "Continue on error" setting: when enabled, pipeline continues even if an iteration fails — essential for this pattern.
Retry policy: retryIntervalInSeconds with backoffMultiplier creates exponential backoff (10s, 20s, 40s for multiplier=2).
Activity output: @activity('CopyData').output.rowsCopied for success, @activity('CopyData').error.message for failures.
Append Variable activity within ForEach accumulates per-source results into an array for the summary notification.

Three separate tenant environments (dev, test, prod) with manual synchronization

Fabric Deployment Pipelines with Dev/Test/Prod stages, parameter rules for data source overrides per stage, and configured deployment rules that auto-bind datasets to stage-specific connections upon promotion
A single workspace with report copies named "Report_DEV", "Report_TEST", "Report_PROD"

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric Deployment Pipelines define stages (Development, Test, Production) with one-click promotion between them. UAT stakeholders access the Test stage workspace for validation. When approved, promoting to Production instantly publishes to 2,000 users. Backward deployment (Prod to Dev) enables pulling production state to fix urgent issues in the dev environment.
Selective deployment: promote individual items or all items — useful when only specific reports are ready.
Deployment Pipelines show comparison between stages: which items are in-sync, modified, or stage-only.

Read all table documentation in the Glue Data Catalog metadata
Export all tables to Excel and use pivot tables for exploration

Copilot generates and executes PySpark or SQL code, displaying results inline. The analyst iterates conversationally — asking follow-up questions, requesting different visualizations, or asking Copilot to explain patterns it finds. No manual coding required.

ul.li: Copilot for notebooks: generates PySpark/SparkSQL code from natural language, executes it, and explains results.
Data profiling prompts: "show statistics for all numeric columns", "find columns with more than 50% nulls", "detect duplicates on primary key".
Copilot can infer column meanings from sample data and provide human-readable descriptions.
Copilot in Power BI reports also enables natural language Q&A for business users against semantic models.

question.title: Workspace Permissions Model
question.scenario: A Fabric workspace serves multiple personas: data engineers who build pipelines and notebooks, data analysts who create reports and semantic models, business users who only view reports, and an external auditor who needs read-only access to specific lakehouse tables (not all data). The team needs to grant minimum required permissions to each persona without over-provisioning access to sensitive financial data in some tables.
question.question-text: Which permission configuration provides least-privilege access for all personas?

choices.choice: Data engineers: Contributor role; Data analysts: Member role; Business users: Viewer role; External auditor: item-level sharing on specific lakehouse tables with read-only SQL endpoint access and OneLake data access roles for table-level restrictions
Give everyone Admin role and rely on individual responsibility
Create separate workspaces per persona and copy shared items between them
Use a single "Member" role for everyone with verbal agreements about what each person should access

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric workspace roles provide coarse-grained access; item-level sharing and OneLake data access roles provide fine-grained table/column restrictions.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Workspace roles define capability levels: Contributor (create/edit items, no sharing/permissions), Member (share items, create reports), Viewer (view reports and items read-only). Data engineers need Contributor to build pipelines. Analysts need Member to create and share reports. Business users need Viewer for report consumption only. The external auditor gets item-level sharing (per-item permissions without workspace role) on specific lakehouse tables, combined with OneLake data access roles that restrict which tables/folders they can query through the SQL endpoint. This is true least-privilege.

ul.li: Workspace roles hierarchy: Admin > Member > Contributor > Viewer — each inherits lower role capabilities.
Item-level sharing: grants access to specific items without any workspace role — ideal for external users.
OneLake data access roles (preview): define which folders/tables within a lakehouse a user can access — SQL endpoint respects these.
Row-level security on semantic models provides additional filtering for business users who share a Viewer role but need different data slices.

question.title: Time Travel and Versioning
question.scenario: A data engineering team accidentally ran a DELETE statement that removed 1 million valid records from a production Delta table. The error was discovered 2 hours later. They need to recover the deleted records without restoring the entire table to a previous state (because other valid writes happened in the intervening 2 hours). The table has Delta log history retention set to 30 days.
question.question-text: Which Delta Lake capability enables selective recovery of the deleted records without losing subsequent valid writes?

choices.choice: Restore the table to the version before the delete using RESTORE, losing all subsequent writes

Use Delta time travel to read the deleted records from the previous version, then INSERT them back into the current table — recovering only the deleted rows while preserving all subsequent valid writes
Recover from the most recent backup snapshot in OneLake
Contact Microsoft support to restore the table from internal backups

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Delta time travel lets you read any historical version — compare the before-delete version to current to identify exactly which records were removed.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Delta time travel (VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF) reads the table state before the erroneous DELETE. By comparing the pre-delete version to the current table (using EXCEPT or LEFT ANTI JOIN), you identify exactly which records were removed. INSERT these recovered records into the current table — restoring only the deleted rows without affecting any valid writes that occurred in the 2 hours since. This is selective recovery: precise, auditable, and non-destructive to subsequent data. RESTORE would overwrite the entire table to a point in time, losing all valid writes after that point.

ul.li: Syntax: SELECT * FROM table VERSION AS OF 42 EXCEPT SELECT * FROM table — gives exactly the deleted rows.
TIMESTAMP AS OF '2026-05-05T10:00:00' — useful when you know the approximate time of the bad operation.
DESCRIBE HISTORY table — shows all operations with version numbers, timestamps, and operation types for forensics.
Time travel requires that VACUUM has not removed the relevant files — default retention is 7 days (168 hours).

question.title: Stream Processing with Eventstream
question.scenario: An e-commerce platform sends clickstream events (page views, add-to-cart, purchases) to Azure Event Hub at 10,000 events/second. The team needs three outputs from this stream: real-time dashboard showing current active users and conversion funnel (updated every 10 seconds), enriched events joined with customer profile data written to the lakehouse for historical analysis, and alerts when the cart abandonment rate exceeds 80% in a 5-minute window.
question.question-text: Which Fabric Eventstream configuration handles all three output requirements from a single input stream?

choices.choice: Three separate Eventstreams each consuming from the same Event Hub independently
Data Pipeline with a scheduled trigger every 10 seconds reading from Event Hub
Spark Structured Streaming notebook processing the stream with three output sinks

Single Eventstream with Event Hub source, branching to: KQL database destination for real-time dashboards, lakehouse destination with custom processing for enrichment, and Data Activator trigger for abandonment rate alerting

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Eventstream supports multiple destinations from a single source — each destination handles a different output pattern.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: A single Eventstream connects to the Event Hub source and routes events to three destinations: KQL database for real-time dashboards (sub-second ingestion, Power BI real-time reporting with auto-refresh), lakehouse destination with inline transformations (joining with customer dimension data for enrichment before landing in Delta tables), and Data Activator for monitoring aggregated metrics (cart abandonment rate over 5-minute windows) with automated Teams/email alerts when thresholds are breached. This single pipeline handles ingestion, enrichment, analytics, and alerting without separate infrastructure per use case.

ul.li: Eventstream supports multiple destinations from a single source — events are replicated to each destination independently.
KQL database ingestion provides sub-second latency — ideal for real-time dashboards with 10-second refresh.
Eventstream inline processing: filter, project, group-by, and join operations on the stream before destination.
Data Activator integration: windowed aggregations (tumbling/hopping windows) feed trigger conditions directly from the stream.

question.title: Semantic Model Refresh Strategy
question.scenario: A semantic model has 20 tables: 2 large fact tables (500M and 300M rows) that change daily, 15 dimension tables (1K to 1M rows) that change rarely (weekly), and 3 reference tables that never change. The current full refresh takes 4 hours and runs nightly. Business users need the fact tables refreshed twice daily (7 AM and 1 PM) but the 4-hour refresh window is too long for midday runs. The model is in Import mode.
question.question-text: Which refresh strategy reduces refresh time while maintaining data freshness for fact tables?

choices.choice: Schedule full refresh 3 times daily and accept the 4-hour processing window
Incremental refresh on fact tables (refresh only recent partitions), static dimensions refreshed weekly on a separate schedule, reference tables excluded from refresh entirely
Switch to DirectQuery to eliminate refresh entirely
Refresh only the 2 fact tables and never refresh dimensions

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Incremental refresh partitions tables by date — only recent partitions are refreshed, reducing time from hours to minutes for large fact tables.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Incremental refresh partitions fact tables by date (e.g., monthly or daily partitions). Only the current and recent partitions are refreshed — historical partitions are untouched. For a 500M-row table where only the last 30 days change, refreshing only those 2-3 partitions takes minutes instead of hours. Dimensions that change weekly are refreshed on a separate weekly schedule. Static reference tables are configured with "never refresh" to avoid unnecessary processing. This reduces the twice-daily refresh from 4 hours to 15-30 minutes.

ul.li: Incremental refresh configuration: define RangeStart/RangeEnd parameters and refresh/archive windows in Power BI.
Detect data changes: polling expression on a modified-date column refreshes a partition only when data actually changed.
XMLA endpoint enables programmatic partition management — refresh specific partitions on demand via API.
Enhanced refresh: "Only refresh complete days" prevents partial day data appearing in reports during the midday refresh.

question.title: Data Science Workflows

Their workflow includes: feature engineering on lakehouse data, model training with scikit-learn and LightGBM, experiment tracking (comparing model versions by accuracy, F1 score), model registration with versioning, and batch scoring that writes predictions back to the lakehouse nightly. question.question-text: Which Fabric capability provides an integrated ML lifecycle without external infrastructure?

choices.choice: Fabric MLflow integration — experiment tracking, model registry, and scoring all within Fabric notebooks using the built-in MLflow server, with results written directly to lakehouse Delta tables
Deploy a separate Azure Machine Learning workspace and connect to Fabric lakehouse via shortcuts
Train models in notebooks and manually save model files to the lakehouse Files section
Use Power BI's built-in AI visuals for all machine learning tasks

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Fabric provides a built-in MLflow integration — no external MLflow server needed for experiment tracking and model management.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric includes a fully managed MLflow integration within notebooks. Data scientists: log experiments (mlflow.log_metric, mlflow.log_param) to track model performance across versions, register best models in the built-in model registry with versioning and stage transitions (Staging, Production), and deploy models for batch scoring in scheduled notebooks that read from and write predictions to lakehouse Delta tables. The MLflow UI (accessible from the workspace) provides experiment comparison, metric visualization, and artifact management — all without external infrastructure.

ul.li: Fabric MLflow: mlflow.set_experiment(), mlflow.start_run(), mlflow.log_metrics() — standard MLflow API works natively.
Model registry: mlflow.register_model() with version tracking, stage transitions (None > Staging > Production > Archived).
Batch scoring: mlflow.pyfunc.load_model() in a scheduled notebook, apply to Spark DataFrame, write to Delta table.
PREDICT function in SQL endpoint allows scoring registered models directly from T-SQL queries (preview feature).

question.title: Tenant-Level Administration
question.scenario: A Fabric tenant admin needs to govern 50 workspaces across 500 users. Concerns include: users creating workspaces without approval, sensitive data being shared externally via Power BI publish-to-web, uncontrolled Spark cluster sizes consuming excessive capacity, and no visibility into which users access which data across the organization. The admin needs centralized controls without blocking legitimate self-service analytics.
question.question-text: Which tenant-level settings balance governance with self-service for this organization?

choices.choice: Block all self-service features and require IT approval for every action
Remove Fabric licenses from all non-IT users to prevent unauthorized usage
Leave all settings at defaults and address issues reactively when they occur

Admin portal settings: restrict workspace creation to security group, disable publish-to-web or restrict to internal domains, configure Spark pool limits per workspace, and enable audit logging with Microsoft Purview for data access tracking — while keeping report creation and data exploration unrestricted for all users

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Tenant settings provide granular controls: restrict risky features to authorized groups while leaving analytical capabilities open for self-service.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Fabric Admin Portal tenant settings enable surgical governance: workspace creation restricted to an "Approved Creators" security group prevents sprawl without blocking existing workspaces. Publish-to-web disabled (or restricted to approved security groups) prevents public data exposure. Spark pool configuration limits (max nodes, auto-scale bounds) prevent runaway capacity consumption. Audit logs (unified audit in Microsoft 365 + Purview) track all data access across the tenant. Meanwhile, report creation, notebook execution, and data exploration remain unrestricted — preserving the self-service analytics experience for all 500 users.

ul.li: Tenant settings apply globally or to specific security groups — enabling graduated rollout of features.
Workspace creation governance: "Users can create workspaces" setting restricted to an AD security group.
Export settings: control whether users can export data from reports (CSV, Excel, PDF) — another data loss prevention lever.
Admin monitoring workspace: auto-created workspace with admin usage metrics semantic model for tracking adoption and governance.

question.title: Lakehouse Security Architecture
question.scenario: A healthcare lakehouse stores patient data subject to HIPAA. Access requirements: doctors can see patient records for their assigned patients only, nurses can see demographics and vitals but not psychiatric notes, researchers can see de-identified data only, and administrators can see everything. All access must be audited with who-what-when logging. The data is in a single lakehouse with 50 tables.
question.question-text: Which layered security approach provides role-based, column-level, and row-level protection with auditing?

choices.choice: Create separate lakehouses per role with different table subsets copied to each

OneLake data access roles for table-level access, column-level security on the SQL endpoint to hide psychiatric columns from nurses, dynamic row-level security in the semantic model for doctor-patient assignment, and audit logs via Fabric activity logging
Application-level security in the reporting tool only, with no lakehouse-level controls
Encrypt sensitive columns and only provide decryption keys to authorized roles

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Layer multiple security mechanisms: table-level (OneLake roles), column-level (SQL endpoint), row-level (semantic model), and audit logging.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Layered security addresses each requirement: OneLake data access roles control which tables each role can access at the storage layer. Column-level security on the SQL analytics endpoint restricts columns (DENY SELECT on psychiatric_notes columns for nurse role). Dynamic RLS in the semantic model filters rows based on doctor-patient assignment (USERPRINCIPALNAME() matched to assignment table). Researchers get a separate view with de-identified columns (hashed patient IDs, removed names). Fabric audit logs capture all data access events with user identity, item accessed, and timestamp for HIPAA compliance.

ul.li: Defense in depth: even if one layer is misconfigured, other layers prevent unauthorized access.
SQL endpoint column-level security: GRANT SELECT on specific columns, DENY on restricted columns per database role.
De-identification for researchers: create views with SHA256(patient_id) as anonymized_id and exclude PII columns.
HIPAA requires 6-year audit retention — configure audit log export to immutable storage for compliance.

question.title: Data Warehouse Loading Patterns
question.scenario: A Fabric Warehouse receives nightly loads from the lakehouse silver layer. The warehouse has a star schema with 5 fact tables and 20 dimension tables. Currently, the load process: truncates and reloads all tables nightly (3 hours), breaks all query caches, causes report errors during the load window, and violates referential integrity temporarily (facts load before dimensions complete). Users need uninterrupted query access during loads.
question.question-text: Which loading pattern eliminates downtime, preserves query performance, and maintains referential integrity?

choices.choice: Load dimensions first in dependency order, then facts — accepting a 3-hour window with stale data

Table swap pattern: load data into staging tables (parallel loads for all tables), validate referential integrity in staging, then use ALTER TABLE SWAP to atomically swap staging with production — zero downtime, instant switch, integrity guaranteed
Use MERGE (upsert) on all tables incrementally instead of truncate and reload
Schedule loads during a maintenance window when no users are active

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: The table swap pattern loads to staging tables while production stays live, then atomically swaps — zero downtime and integrity validation before swap.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The table swap pattern: create staging versions of all tables, load data into staging (all tables in parallel since order doesn't matter for staging), run referential integrity validation queries on staging tables (ensuring foreign keys resolve), then execute ALTER TABLE SWAP to atomically replace production tables with staging. Users experience zero downtime — queries hit production tables until the instant of swap. Referential integrity is validated before go-live. Query caches are preserved for the most recent queries since the swap is instant. If validation fails, production remains untouched — no partial load corruption.

ul.li: ALTER TABLE SWAP in Fabric Warehouse: atomic metadata operation — instant regardless of table size.
Parallel staging loads: all 25 tables load simultaneously (no dependency ordering needed since staging is independent).
Integrity validation: SELECT fact.dim_key WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM dim WHERE dim.key = fact.dim_key) should return 0 rows.
Rollback: keep the previous production tables (renamed) for 24 hours — instant rollback by swapping back if issues are found.

question.title: Multi-Language Semantic Model
question.scenario: A global company deploys Power BI reports to users in 12 countries. Reports must display measure names, column headers, and table names in each user's local language (English, French, German, Spanish, Japanese, etc.). The underlying data values remain in English but all metadata (field names, folder names, measure display names) must be translated. Managing 12 separate semantic models is not sustainable.
question.question-text: Which approach provides multi-language metadata in a single semantic model?

choices.choice: Translations in the semantic model using the TMDL/TMSL translation properties — a single model with metadata translated into multiple cultures, displayed based on the user's browser locale
Create 12 copies of the semantic model with translated field names in each
Use calculated columns with SWITCH on user language for display names
Create a translation lookup table and use DAX to dynamically rename columns

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Tabular model translations are a built-in feature — metadata (captions) can be defined per culture/locale in a single model.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Tabular model translations (TMDL translations property) define translated captions, descriptions, and display folder names for each supported culture (en-US, fr-FR, de-DE, es-ES, ja-JP, etc.) within a single semantic model. Power BI Service automatically displays the appropriate translation based on the user's browser locale setting. This is a metadata-only feature — no data duplication, no separate models, no DAX complexity. Translators maintain a translation file (JSON) that maps each object to its localized name. Tools like Tabular Editor and ALM Toolkit provide UI for managing translations.

ul.li: Translations apply to: table names, column names, measure names, hierarchy names, level names, and display folders.
TMDL format: model/tables/Sales/translations/fr-FR.tmdl defines French translations for the Sales table.
Tabular Editor 3: Translation Manager view provides a grid UI for bulk translation management across all cultures.
Fallback: if a translation is missing for the user's locale, the default culture (usually en-US) is displayed.

question.title: Power BI Embedded Analytics
question.scenario: A SaaS company wants to embed Fabric Power BI reports into their customer-facing web application. Requirements: each customer sees only their own data (multi-tenant isolation), the embedding must work without customers needing Power BI licenses, the application controls authentication (customers log in to the SaaS app, not to Microsoft), and reports must be white-labeled (no Power BI branding visible).
question.question-text: Which Power BI embedding approach meets all requirements for customer-facing SaaS analytics?

choices.choice: "User Owns Data" embedding requiring each customer to have a Power BI Pro license and Microsoft account

Power BI Embedded with "App Owns Data" pattern — service principal authentication, generate embed tokens with effective identity for RLS enforcement per customer, embedded in an iframe with custom branding
Publish reports to Power BI public web (publish-to-web) with URL parameters for filtering
Export reports as PDF per customer and display in the web application

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: "App Owns Data" with service principal and effective identity provides multi-tenant embedding without customer licenses.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: "App Owns Data" pattern: the SaaS application authenticates to Power BI using a service principal (no user interaction with Microsoft). The app generates embed tokens with EffectiveIdentity specifying the customer's tenant ID — Power BI applies RLS rules to show only that customer's data. Customers interact with fully interactive reports embedded in iframes within the SaaS UI — no Power BI license needed per user. Custom CSS and configuration hide Power BI branding. The Fabric capacity (F-SKU) provides the compute — cost is per-capacity, not per-user.

ul.li: Service principal: registered in Azure AD, granted workspace Member role — no interactive user needed for embedding.
EffectiveIdentity in embed token: specifies username and roles — RLS evaluates as that identity without actual user authentication.
F-SKU (Fabric) replaces A-SKU (Azure) and EM-SKU (Premium) for embedded scenarios — single capacity type for all workloads.
Client-side APIs (powerbi-client JavaScript SDK) enable: page navigation, bookmark application, filter setting, and event handling in the host application.

question.title: Performance Troubleshooting
question.scenario: A Power BI report that was fast last week now takes 45 seconds to load. Nothing changed in the report definition. The data volume grew by 10% (within normal range). The semantic model uses DirectLake mode connected to a lakehouse Delta table. Users report the slowdown started on Monday morning. The Fabric capacity utilization shows normal levels. The DBA confirms no changes to the underlying data pipeline.
question.question-text: What is the most likely cause and how should it be diagnosed?

choices.choice: DirectLake fallback to DirectQuery due to exceeding guardrail limits (max rows, model size) — diagnose via DAX query plan showing DirectQuery mode, resolve by running OPTIMIZE on the Delta table to compact files and reduce row group count, or increase DirectLake guardrail limits for the capacity
The Fabric capacity is throttled — upgrade to a larger SKU
The Power BI service is experiencing a global outage affecting all tenants
Network latency between the user's browser and the Power BI service increased

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: DirectLake silently falls back to DirectQuery when guardrails are exceeded — small data growth can push a table over the threshold, causing dramatic performance drops.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: DirectLake has guardrails: maximum rows per table, maximum model size, and maximum column cardinality. When exceeded, DirectLake silently falls back to DirectQuery mode — generating SQL queries against the SQL endpoint instead of reading Parquet files directly. This causes dramatic performance degradation (from seconds to 45+ seconds). The 10% data growth likely pushed the table over a guardrail limit. Additionally, if OPTIMIZE hasn't run on the Delta table, accumulated small files increase the Parquet row group count beyond DirectLake's file-per-table limit. Diagnosis: check the DAX query plan for "DirectQuery" storage mode on tables that should be DirectLake.

ul.li: DirectLake guardrails per F-SKU: F2 supports 300M rows/table, F64 supports 1.5B rows — check capacity-specific limits.
Diagnose: DAX Studio query plan shows StorageMode per table — "DirectLake" is healthy, "DirectQuery" indicates fallback.
Resolution options: OPTIMIZE Delta table (compact files), increase capacity SKU (higher guardrails), or reduce model scope.
Framing status: if framing failed (could not load Parquet segments), DirectLake falls back for all queries until successful framing.
